Document · 1983

Speaking of Conan

Hayao Miyazaki · 31 October 1983
Mata aeta, ne! (“We Meet Again!”) ed. Yōkō Tomizawa, Animage bunko, October 31, 1983 · from Starting Point: 1979–1996, Hayao Miyazaki (VIZ Media, 2009)

Interviewer: Yōko TomizawaMata aeta, ne! (“We Meet Again!”) ed. Yōkō Tomizawa, Animage bunko, October 31, 1983

Directorial Debut with Conan

—Miyazaki-san, you made your directorial debut with Future Boy Conan. In retrospect, how was it?

Miyazaki: It was tough, frankly. I’d been working with Paku-san (Isao Takahata) up to then, you see. In watching him, I really thought that directing wasn’t for me, because a director has to assume such a heavy individual responsibility. Seeing what directing involved made me not try it up until then.

—But you had drawn storyboards before, hadn’t you? For example, in the Akadō Suzunosuke animated TV series?

Miyazaki: Yes, but that sort of thing’s easy to do. And the easier something is, the easier it is for me to motivate myself. It was just a silly story, without anything particularly good or bad about it. Rather than focusing on something twisted, it was just a warm story, the sort of thing that evokes a bunch of chuckles and then ends. I think this is true of lots of manga, so in this case it’s probably better to call Akadō Suzunosuke a cartoon film, rather than animation.

—I worked on the in-between animation for Conan, and I have to say I was really happy to be able to work on the project. Everybody had really wanted to work on something that was fun and liberating, especially since before Conan we had worked on From the Apennines to the Andes. It’s a really wonderful work, too, but the content is pretty serious, so I and my friends from the production team had talked about how we hoped to work on something a bit more upbeat and fun next.

Miyazaki: I’m the same way, in the sense that I normally like to work on upbeat and fun stories. As you know, we animators have to work all day at our desks. So we don’t really have any good way to work off our stress. But when some of the drawings depict really wacky and fun stuff, it works as a type of stress reliever for us. If there’s some slapstick sequence in a very introspective play, for example, or if there’s a clear contrast between stillness and motion, slow and fast, or explosiveness and silence, then both aspects really come alive. If the overall tempo has already been established, those working on the film inevitably become much more passive. Of course, it’s also suffocating for us if everything is done in slapstick style.

—What was it about Conan that made the directing so difficult for you? Did it have something to do with the directions the producer gave you?

Miyazaki: I was frankly in a dilemma after my work on From the Apennines to the Andes ended. I really thought I could never do any work that involved just layouts. But then I was asked if I’d like to try directing. Even today I don’t like being pegged just as a “director” or as someone who just does scene designs or screen layouts. Rather than being seen solely as directing, if it’s something that I like to work on, I’d actually like to be thought of as an animator.

—So you mean you’d like to create your own world …

Miyazaki: Yes, that’s right. Up till now, things have gone really well, because everything I’ve wanted to do has fit really well with Paku-san. Looking back on it, of course I’m sure Paku-san was at times frustrated. Even times when I thought everything was going great, he was often grumbling all over the place about what directing animation films was supposed to really mean. Up until now, when I’ve worked with Paku-san, we’ve discussed everything in detail, from the core story to what we should do and how; usually while lazily lying about, we come up with some sort of shared image of what we want to do, then talk about drawing it. That’s how we work. But from around the time of the Heidi TV series, the screen design and layout work alone started to take up so much time that I would never have been able maintain any sort of schedule. So for From the Apennines to the Andes I handed it all off to Paku-san. But in doing that, of course, I was the one who started to feel frustrated.

—So that brings us to Conan, doesn’t it? Did it move along according to schedule?

Miyazaki: We had more than six months between when we started drawing the key animation for the first episode and when it went on air. And in that time, despite the fact that we started with a stock of eight episodes ready, we still wound up slipping behind the broadcast schedule. No matter what we did, we found that it took us from ten days to two weeks to produce a single episode. If NHK hadn’t inserted a special program in there as padding, it probably would have turned into a real wreck of a series. If we hadn’t been working for NHK, we never could have pulled Conan off. NHK let us do everything the way we wanted to; sometimes we even created the scripts after we had created the storyboards. To create sixteen episodes we ultimately took a year and three months. I think the company (Nippon Animation) probably went heavily into the red on production costs.

—Did you have a prep period for production?

Miyazaki: That’s something I remember clearly; we had about three months, because on June 15 I pulled out of doing original drawings for Araiguma rasukaru (Rascal Raccoon), declaring that I was off that job starting the next day, and we started doing the key animation for Conan around the end of that summer.

—In the interim were you able to do the overall layout for Conan?

Miyazaki: Well, yes and no. To tell the truth, I had only mentally done the layout up to the part where he goes into the desert to rescue Lana. Beyond that I just figured that it would all work out somehow … We had a scenario up to the meeting with Doctor Lao, which was a big turning point, but the world the story was set in hadn’t been fully created then, so Paku-san handled the work based on the scenario for episodes nine and ten. I was at my limit then, physically speaking. Dyce and Conan were supposed to get on the Barracuda and escape, and while on the ship and heading for High Harbor, they would get into a silly fuss over Lana and the story would mainly be about that. But there was no way it would work. So instead we featured the Core Block.

Balancing the work with the original story

—You mean that you were pulled along by the darker quality of the original story?

Miyazaki: In the beginning I didn’t want to be constrained by the original story. The theme was really too scary. I felt there was no way that I could properly take it on. But then my son was watching television, and he asked me who the underground-dwellers really were. He was concerned about the people of Plaschip Island and wondering what would happen to them. So then I got worried. I still think of this series as basically a love story between Conan and Lana, but without depicting this part of the story properly, Conan and Lana would never have amounted to anything more than two people with crushes on each other. I realized what was missing, but I really didn’t know what to do about it. I had accepted the original idea of a post-Armageddon setting for an adventure story, but I did feel constrained by the burden of the heavy ending.

You probably remember the scene in episode seven with all the hands coming out of the jail—it makes you wonder who all those guys are. Sort of like solving a puzzle. The relationships are all inverted, so at that point you have to start asking the characters who they really are and what they’re doing. No one on the staff, including me, knew where we were going to be led. It was a disastrous situation. It sounds pathetic to say this, but it’s really true that, if you don’t have the A part of the story done, it’s hard to know what the B part will be. So to tell you the truth, we just figured to hell with the directorial plan. We talked about making it an emotive type of animation, and it turned out to be moving in an emotionally unstable direction. But that was the only way we could deal with that story.

—Did NHK choose the story?

Miyazaki: NHK said that they wanted to start an animated TV series, so Nippon Animation apparently presented them with a few proposals. And among them was Alexander Key’s story, The Incredible Tide. NHK at first apparently favored a different story, but then they came out and said that this one was more interesting. So this proposal was actually not the first that came to me.

—Alexander Key’s The Incredible Tide is actually a fairly dark story, isn’t it?

Miyazaki: I think that the dark quality of the original story comes from the author’s intrinsically dark worldview. And in discussing the subject, it’s probably hard to come up with a very optimistic answer. I think we may also see the story as dark because we live in Japan. That aside, I think it is still something we probably need to talk about. In a post-apocalyptic world, any human survivors would obviously have to possess a very powerful will to live. I know I’d want that for my own children. Rather than be told that the human race is going to be destroyed, I know I’d much rather have my son thrilled by the girls he sees around him and chasing after them.

—What were your thoughts on the relationship between the animated series and the original story?

Miyazaki: Well, my thoughts on the connection between the two are if you’re dealing with a work with such a high level of perfection that it requires a very strict interpretation, then you’re better off not trying to turn it into a cartoon series in the first place. It’s probably better to think of the original story as just the trigger for the ideas in the cartoon series. I think of the project plan as simply being a vessel; figuring out what to put into the vessel is part of my job.

—So in the case of this work, you felt it was probably all right to change the story?

Miyazaki: Yes, and it was something I decided to do on my own. At the time, NHK apparently had some concern about their relationship with the story’s author, but I had only accepted the work on the condition that I would be able to make changes.

—You made some major changes, didn’t you?

Miyazaki: I didn’t like the original story. It’s too pessimistic and too tangled up with ideas about America and the Soviet Union. The author’s views of an End Times or Armageddon come from his own latent insecurities and fears, so he brought an awful lot of this pessimism with him, and I had some serious doubts about the appropriateness of this in a series for children. Even if someone’s lost all hope for the future, I still think it’s incredibly stupid to go around stressing this to children. Emphasize it to adults it you have to, but there’s no need to do so to children. It would be better to simply not say anything at all.

It seems to me that Key wrote the story believing that modern America’s basically no good, and that the Soviet Union isn’t either, but he doesn’t really know what to do, so he’s working on an assumption that a survivor might turn into something like a King Conan. But there’s not a shred of hope there, or even much vitality in the characters. Key puts all of his energy into the negative aspects, and in one sense it’s easy to write about the negatives. In real life, humans are filled with weaknesses and cowardice after all. But that’s not what I want to depict.

In the original story, you have what seems to me to be a world without hope. You have a weird society where people dream of riding bicycles through desolate scenes of dark oceans, gray skies, and craggy boulders and rocks—it’s a bleak mental landscape. And you have this weird society called High Harbor. I don’t think a boy like Conan would ever have been born in a world like that. Nature recovers and forgives humans, and even though “forgives” is a strange way to put it, I do think that nature creates the foundation for all life to exist, so that humans (who are also animals) can go on living. Conversely, in creating the setting for a character like Conan, I think it would have been better to have had nature having already made its comeback. I have been told, however, that the idea that nature can recover by itself may be a very Japanese one … It’s sort of like cutting down a tree: when you do, you later get an explosion of weeds and brush, right? But in the real world, there are lots of places where, after you cut down the trees, you wind up with nothing growing at all. And I don’t think any people living in such a place could ever make the sorts of things they have in the story. After Armageddon, if the survivors were going to go on living with a lot of duds among them, unless nature itself recovered, humanity would soon go extinct.

—So that’s why, in the animated TV series, you set the story twenty years after an Armageddon and assumed that blue skies and clean oceans have returned to earth, right?

Miyazaki: Yes. I incorporated my own hopes in the work. It may seem odd to say this, but those lines in the animated story—where Dr. Lao talks about taking responsibility for having killed billions of humans and exterminated tens of thousands of animal and plant species—are personally meaningful to me.

I really wanted to make all the characters Japanese and, if not Japanese, at least have them all the same nationality so we could totally forget about language barriers; to differentiate characters visually we did have some red-haired people appear, but I basically wanted to avoid having different races of people in the story. Also, even if Japan were to sink out of sight, I thought it would be good to at least have a tip of Japan’s Bōsō peninsula, or some vast industrial complex, survive. In other words, in a story like this there is a problem with distance, because if there is no means of transportation, and we have a totally unknown world, then everything seems really far away. I also think it would have been better to show people at High Harbor growing rice in paddies rather than wheat in fields, but if I had tried to do this too many other problems would have emerged.

We wound up with the world you see in the series because, if we had tried to make what I had originally wanted, there would have been too many other rules to follow. And we’d have lost any flexibility in the production. For the sake of the staff I also thought we had no choice but to create a world with a common language. I frankly feel a little frustrated by the fact that the world of Conan turned out looking a bit like the American West. I think it would have been perfect if instead of the Barracuda ship, we’d had an old Japanese fishing boat called the Bentenmaru, and instead of knives and forks, we’d had chopsticks and china bowls, the characters demanding food in Japanese, saying, “Meshi!”

In the original story the whole focus on the Soviet Union and America represents a type of arrogance, and I really hate it. And therefore it really bugs me that—despite all my efforts to eliminate this perspective from the story—some people still say that High Harbor represents America and Industria represents the Soviet Union. Thinking of the Soviet Union or of the United States in those terms is in itself a problem.

—On the subject of Conan, I can’t help but think about the connection to Little Norse Prince Valiant.

Miyazaki: I can’t say anything about Little Norse Prince Valiant. Really, I can’t. I know this’ll sound conceited, but you’re talking about my own youth. The film’s got everything I feel embarrassed about in it. Both Paku-san and I were able to work on that film then precisely because we were so young. I’ve already said more than I should have, things that are unspeakably embarrassing. We wanted to depict humanity … We were burning with ambition then.

With Conan, at first I really didn’t know what I should do. I thought of creating a healthy, traditional type of adventure story, the sort that isn’t done much in animation these days, what we hadn’t been able to do fully in Little Norse Prince Valiant. I wanted to have a young protagonist who takes over from the failed generation of older guys. There are all types of failures, of course, and what I actually like vis-à-vis the next generation is not just negating what your own generation has done but transmitting something to the future, or passing it on. Now, I’m certainly not in a position to talk in a high-minded way to my own sons about passing anything on, but, conversely, that may also be a reason that I always have this in mind.

When we started working on Conan, I would have quit the animation business if people had thought that what we were trying to do was boring. But to my surprise even my sons became passionate fans of the show. Now, I know their opinions alone aren’t worth much, but at least they aren’t the type of kids who just watch shows because their dad’s working on them …

—Ratings for the show weren’t very good, were they …

Miyazaki: Right. Episode twenty-five got the highest rating, of 14 percent. But I can sort of understand why the overall series ratings weren’t so good. We were creating something that went against the grain of the times. Of course, some people later said that the ratings would have been a bit better if we had shown more of the Giganto plane flying earlier in the story. As you know, Conan and Lana first come across the plane in a hangar, but then we totally forget about it until it takes off. Rather than having it fly from the beginning, however, I thought that spending two cours leading up to the take-off would have more impact. I have to say, though, I’ve never worried about ratings as much as I did with this show. The production staff really did their best for it.

—Because there hadn’t been many tightly serialized stories like Conan before, do you suppose people had a hard time keeping up if they missed an episode?

Miyazaki: Well, as I mentioned earlier, you can’t create the B part of a show without first creating the A part. I think it’s usually true of everything, but we see and hear a lot of things and store the information in our heads, right? Later, we may not be able to recall it all exactly as it occurred, but if we really wrack our brains, some of the stuff comes floating up, lots of elements collect, and sometimes they create a unified thread. But with Conan this was always a problem. So I pulled out all sorts of things and opened them up, but it just drove me crazier than ever. The only thing I did know is that Conan was the one who would ultimately return to Remnant Island. And since he was going to return, I knew that he was a really tough kid who could do all sorts of things. In the last episode, I was really happy to see Remnant Island reappear in the film. I really felt like Conan had come home. Because for a while I thought he’d never make it.

—Was the matter of the cigarettes the only restriction that NHK put on you?

Miyazaki: Actually, in the beginning NHK said they didn’t mind. But then, just before we aired, they apparently had some sort of problem with cigarettes on a different program. I had intended for that smoking scene to be the only one in the movie and had planned to depict it in a good way. We had designed the character of the boy Jimsy to be someone who ran about full of energy in the midst of a post-apocalyptic wasteland, so I had of course assumed that he would smoke cigarettes. He’s supposed to be someone who gets all of his own food, even if he has to barter for it, so I had assumed that he would at least want some cigarettes. I have to say, it still makes me angry to think that I didn’t know they had edited this part out until the show was actually broadcast … Still, I have to admit that I would also have been angry if I’d known in advance they were going to cut the scene out, and then had to redo it.

The first episode

—When I happened to see a screening of the first episode at NHK, I thought it was truly fantastic!

Miyazaki: The first episode? To tell you the truth, when I first saw it, I thought of hanging myself. At Cinebeam, the recording studio, there’s a graveyard out back and a hanging rope … [laughs] I thought that Lana should be so beautiful that Conan would want to devote his life to her the instant he spied her, but the Lana that appeared on the screen was so very unbeautiful!

—The first episode was based entirely on Yasuo Ōtsuka-san’s drawings, wasn’t it?

Miyazaki: Yes, it was. I went nuts after that. After the first episode I insisted on checking all the key animation, and did that up until episode eight. Ōtsuka-san developed quite a complex about it. I’m an animator, see? When Conan was supposed to lift up Lana, he should have gently lifted her up, like a bird, but Ōtsuka-san is an ultra-logical person, so he had Conan heave Lana up, almost with a one-two-three. I’ve grumbled that this scene actually represents Ōtsuka-san lifting up his own wife.

In Heidi, we had started showing characters walking in different ways, with shortened steps, or with a quick pace, or in a way that seems to go on forever. But in most traditional cartoon movies, the characters reach the horizon in about three steps. For example, I love the cartoon character Farmer Alfalfa who practically comes bounding at us. It’s something you can only depict in cartoons. You’d never be able to do it in live action. So I think that it’s really a shame to relinquish these original attributes of animation. If the character’s running at full speed, I want him or her to be depicted running faster than any normal human could ever run. For me, this is an expression of style. Up until Conan, most Japanese animation had very slow timing or pacing, and in this sense I think many people found our style quite confusing. They probably found it to be maddeningly busy. This continued for a long time, even among the production staff members.

Designing Conan

—Is the Conan character a type of ideal boy for you, or did you design him to be a character you wished you could have been?

Miyazaki: That’s a tough question to answer. But I can say that I like boy characters like Conan. They always make me think about how old children are when they start imagining themselves as the heroes in their own fantasy stories. It seems to me that most boys are about eleven when they start imagining themselves as the heroes in stories where they have traditional roles like saving princesses, etc., so that’s why I made Conan eleven. Of course there’s always something a bit half-baked about all this, because when my son turned twelve I always told him Conan was twelve, too. I merely wanted to give shape and form to the hopes and dreams of children. But I don’t think that in this story we literally have to think of the characters’ age as being the same rapidly growing eleven or twelve as in the real world. Both Conan and Lana sometimes behave as adults, and sometimes as children, but in the world of cartoons I think that’s okay.

—If you watch Conan with girls, they all say that he’s an ideal type of male character. He’s always very gentle and kind.

Miyazaki: I think everyone feels that way; we’d probably all like to meet a person who would make us want to do our best for her, who would make us feel truly gentle toward her. Don’t you think so? I think so. Now, I’m not talking about meeting someone with whom you would want to take oaths of loyalty and spend the rest of your life—that’s something of an entirely different dimension. Of course, we’re lucky that in this world there are relatively few females who can drive men out of their minds and make them want to act so gently. That sort of thing should be limited to crushes. And infatuation. It’s like the world Sōji Yamakawa depicts in his illustrated story Shōnen Ōja (The Boy King), isn’t it? Ah, the days when you could get away with that were great.

Conan’s not a superman. He’s an ordinary kid who mainly thinks about having fun in his life. But humans are complex characters. And one fact about Conan is that the conditions in which he lives amplify certain aspects of his personality. He doesn’t go out looking for adventure; he just does his best to stay alive in the conditions in which he finds himself. Conan sees the world through Lana, and Lana sees the world through Dr. Lao. And ultimately, Conan comes to embody what is most important in the world in which he lives. Even though he doesn’t express it verbally, he comes to embody the vitality, resolute spirit, and understanding of others that his world needs. I personally like the idea that it is because of Conan’s silent influence that Jimsy becomes happier, that Dyce tries to become more normal, and that Monsley is transformed.

Some people say that Conan’s too much of a goodie-two-shoes, but rather than an always-innocent, happy-go-lucky Conan, I prefer to think of him as he is in episode twenty-three, when he sees the Flying Machine explode and doesn’t exclaim, “Yay!” Instead, he feels the full weight of having actually killed other people. I like him because I see him as a boy who gets angry but doesn’t have a murderous streak in him. I didn’t want him to exclaim “Yay!” when the Gunboat sank, either. It’s probably only true of this series, but I don’t care if some viewers feel like saying “Yay, he did it!” or “Serves ’em right,” but having him say “Banzai!” just didn’t seem to fit with his personality. Of course, I’m sure that some will criticize this and still say that he’s too much of a goodie-two-shoes or that he doesn’t have enough vitality as a character. But I don’t think he could have overcome all the problems he faces unless he had the sort of personality he does. He’s the kind of hero you typically find in cartoon movies and adventure stories. Frankly, I don’t like the sort of people who say he’s “too good.” I’m tempted to say to them, “So you want to see bad kids, you fool?” I know that we weren’t always able to adequately express Conan’s various moods or properly show the qualities he embodied, but even so, I think it’s all right to have a truly good guy—someone who’s truly likeable—in a story like this. In looking at recent shows with a mecha orientation, the protagonist is often a young male between boyhood and youth who, when told something by his unit commander or a professor, replies cheekily with, “Hey, I already knew that!” like a teenage son still in his rebellious stage. When I see that sort of thing, the characters seem so obnoxious I feel like knocking them down. I frankly just can’t see that sort of young male as a hero.

A special fondness for Lana

—What do you think of Lana? To me, she seems like your vision of the ideal heroine, especially in the eighth episode of the series.

Miyazaki: Well, I think I put way too much of my own feelings into episode eight. I did everything I wanted to do my own way, which I absolutely never would have been able to do had I been working with Paku-san. Some people have of course criticized me saying I went overboard. And when I put together the first scripts for the show I, too, frankly thought they were too embarrassing to produce. But by episodes five and six, I had grown fonder and fonder of Lana. And that made it possible for me to continue. I wouldn’t have been able to make the show without feeling this way about her. When I thought about the underwater scenes after we had finished them, I realized that they incorporated the exact same story line of a manga that I had created back in my student days. In other words, it had been buried for fifteen years. Even the shots were arranged the same way—the only difference was that a hydrofoil I had floating on the horizon in the original had been turned into the Gunboat.

But I eventually resolved my feelings for Lana. In the beginning, I created her thinking that she was mine, but as we went along I came to see that she belonged to Conan. My interest in her started to fade. The whole thing’s a world of pretend anyway. When a ship sinks in the story, for example, there’s no way that only one room in it would be unaffected, and it probably would have been blown out of the water in the subsequent explosion. But I have to say that I like that sort of thing. I like it, for example, where in episode eleven, you may remember, Conan boards the Flying Machine and hands over his effects, and Lana takes them without saying anything more than “hai.” And in episode twenty-three, when Conan leaps on top of the Flying Machine and says, “Open the top hatch,” and Lana opens it, again with a simple “hai.”

In the original story, I think Lana was the kind of character who really wanted the weaving machines that Dyce had brought. She didn’t want to weave anything by hand. But I don’t see that sort of personality connecting well with the future.

—So that’s why you had her changing clothes at High Harbor and weaving by hand?

Miyazaki: Well, I just wanted her to change clothes. Because I think the Lana who is in that wheat field is the real Lana. That episode, fourteen, may not have been very well received, but I like it. That’s Lana, as far as I’m concerned. That’s the Lana to whom I’m attached.

—And she wears the same clothes when she goes to Remnant Island, doesn’t she?

Miyazaki: Yes, she does. And some people have said they make her look like a bit of a hick, despite the fact that I told our colorist to make them look better. The colorist also liked the look of Jimsy’s baggy mompe52 trousers because they’d recently become fashionable. It was a fleeting moment of being liberated, and I wanted to emphasize that freedom … And I have to say, haven’t you ever had an experience similar to that of a kid, a bundle of complexes, who finds himself staring, amazed, at the sight of a girl wearing a white hat and long skirt zipping by on a bicycle right in front of him? It’s a feeling of extraordinary longing and frustration, an awareness of another world that is out of reach. I have memories like that from elementary and junior high school, and I would have loved to have run like Conan in the show, carrying a girl like that. I’m quite shameless about it.

—I suppose it was done out of your fondness for Lana, but early in the series, you had her deliberately change her clothes and come riding out on a bicycle, despite the fact that Monsley was appearing in the Industria harbor.

Miyazaki: No, not out of special fondness, not then, at least. [laughs] Lana originally had a somewhat darker aspect to her character, but she was always concerned about Dr. Lao. Then Conan suddenly lifts her up in his arms and starts running with her. At that point it’s as if she’s always been an upbeat girl, but Conan is the one who actually brings out this part of her personality. To Lana, Conan is like a kid from another dimension; she has to change because of the way he suddenly acts toward her.

Lana is basically torn between her feelings for her grandfather—Dr. Lao—and her feelings for Conan. When she’s with Conan, she’s clearly very upbeat and smiling, but in a corner of her mind she’s also always worried about her grandfather. When she has both Dr. Lao and Conan beside her, that’s when she’s happiest of all. In fact, in episode eleven, Lana becomes such an upbeat kid that she probably seems like a bit of an idiot. But when Triangle Tower is liberated and all the underground residents freed, Lana is the only one who’s held back. Because of her concern for Dr. Lao, her heart starts to close up and she eventually stops being able to hear Conan. Actually, Lana herself realizes what’s happening and wants to flee, but is unable.

Lao, however, realizes what’s happening and that he has no choice but to tell Lana to go to Conan, that it’s okay to leave him. With this he frees her. And when that happens, it seems to me that Lao has to die, and the line where Lana says to the dying Lao, “Conan would stop them,” seems evidence to me that she is gradually shifting away from her grandfather. Without the death of Lao, Lana can never really be free. She would always have had a complex about her grandfather. I think Conan probably knew this, too. That’s why, in scenes—as in episode eight—where he lifts Lana up on top of the tank, it seems to me apparent that Dr. Lao must have had an amazing amount of anger toward other people.

Whether we’re talking about Mao Zedong or others, it’s always the bad guys who try to change history dramatically, so in that sense I think Dr. Lao is essentially an evil character. He felt responsible for the destruction of the previous world, and has been living down his shame by trying to act as a bridge for the next generation. But if the people of Industria hadn’t had the power to free themselves—in other words, if Luke and the others had lacked the power to rise up on their own, escape from the underground, and try to start new lives … if they had instead had to rely on Lao or Conan for their freedom—I think Lao probably would have left them to their own devices and let them sink into the sea. He has this sort of hard-heartedness to him, and under certain circumstances he might not even have been willing to let Lana go. I don’t think Lao is a humanist. I didn’t want any humanists in the show.

People often cave in when hostages are taken or when innocents are threatened. They cave in even before they have any idea of what’s going to happen. Take the example of the film Gamera. Two boys are taken hostage and the entire Earth Defense Forces surrender, right? I think this is totally inexcusable. I believe you shouldn’t surrender even if tens of thousands of people have been taken hostage. I prefer people who have something they’ll never surrender, who don’t give in. And it could be the heroine, or anything. When Lepka turns a tattoo gun on Conan, she could lie. She could say that she’d cooperate, but if she’s not as cynical about the world as we are—and if she’s a particularly upright girl—then I think she probably wouldn’t just try to get out of whatever temporary jam she was in, but also to defiantly defend herself. In fact, for me to use Lana as a heroine, she has to be able to defend herself.

Monsley and Dyce

—I can certainly understand your attachment to Lana, but in the second half of the series, you seem to give more attention to Monsley.

Miyazaki: We used to call it “emotional animation.” I should have calculated more calmly what I wanted to express in directing the film, but I tend to proceed on an emotional basis. I can’t do the work unless I have an emotional investment in it. I tend to pour myself into the characters. And when I do so, I start to empathize with the characters, to feel sorry for them. Monsley’s such a sad case that she nearly brought tears to my eyes. So then I started feeling that I ought to do something to help her out. In trying to help her, I started to think that it would be great if she could fall in love with Conan, but Lana already existed, so that wouldn’t work. And if that’s not possible, then I thought of having her marry Dyce, but at that instant her eyes would have sparkled too much. In other words, she’d just turn into an ordinary woman.

I like women like Monsley. They look tough and defiant, but say they’re waiting for someone to make them change. When I see someone like that, I always feel like saying something gentle to them. I think what happens with people like that is not that they change while being defiant, but that they get to the point where they no longer need to be defiant. And in order for them to change, I think they need someone to appear who really understands what they’re being defiant about—I don’t mean understanding the details of why they’re being defiant, but understanding what’s beneath the surface of their existence. Maybe this makes the person able to smash a barricade of some sort on her own. And Dyce wasn’t the one to do it.

—Did you always harbor that sort of schoolgirlish idea for her?

Miyazaki: Well, there’s no sense in giving away all my secrets, but I do think that Monsley had forgotten everything. People tend to forget everything they don’t want to recall. But in Monsley’s case, seeing the greenery of High Harbor probably made her despondent, and since the Gunboat had been sunk, she probably recalled that she’d been saved by the Gunboat, and then recalled her childhood.

—What about the idea of Monsley marrying Dyce?

Miyazaki: That was first suggested as a joke, and I immediately also thought that it could be interesting. But then I realized that I would have to have Monsley start to think that Dyce might not be such a bad person at all. That’s the problem with Dyce. We had to gradually reveal his good qualities, and in the end this worked quite well. When Monsley becomes a more normal woman, and when she’s freed from the tension that she’s always felt, and no longer has to restrain herself all the time, then she’s able to view things that might have once seemed utterly idiotic to her. Dyce is a total fool, and from the beginning Monsley’s always referring to him as “stupid” or “fool.” But while she’s using these words, the meaning of them starts to change, and Dyce starts to accept this. So both their views change.

I think the way Dyce so consistently tries to take such good care of his ship works in his favor. Monsley is probably moved by the fact that he won’t give up his ship, especially the line he utters about being a “sailor who’ll die in the sky,” and when he stays behind she probably starts to see his good qualities. And after Dyce carries Monsley on his back and gets off the line about her being heavier than Lana, she probably starts to think that things are going too far, but that there’s no turning back. I think the fact that Monsley’s able to go along with this without any big problem shows that she’s capable of leaving behind the always-defiant side of her personality. And for her, becoming a normal person represents a type of liberation.

I could have had Monsley dump Dyce in the end, but I would have felt too sorry for him, especially since so many of the crew members already had new babies by that point. At the wedding, Dyce at first suspects that he might have done something totally ridiculous, then after a bit he really thinks he’s done something ridiculous. We thought about having Dyce act like Dyce to the bitter end, but I think the way he got married was completely in character. When he looks at Monsley he suddenly gets serious, and even starts to look a bit gallant and dignified. Of course, in such a situation, I think anyone starts to look a little dignified. Still, in spite of that, I think that Dyce is definitely the kind of guy who, if a beautiful woman were standing next to him, would think how wonderful she is, and then in the next breath go off and try to make a pass at someone else without getting caught. That’s the kind of man he is. That’s why he assumed that serious expression.

If the show’s viewers don’t get this, they’ll wonder why everything ended with Dyce all of a sudden appearing to have gone serious and straight. I sometimes think they don’t get it. Some members of the production staff thought the very smart and capable Monsley was too good for a man like Dyce. He is, after all, the sort of insincere man that married women tend to distrust, while middle-aged men understand where he’s coming from as they’re often living the same half-baked lives. Dyce is a professional sailor, but he only appears capable and talented when he’s actually captaining the Barracuda because that’s when he’s serious. I can really understand a man like him, who wears his emotions on his sleeve. In the beginning the idea was to make him a bad guy and to have him try to keep winning Lana over up to the end, even in High Harbor. But there was no way that a jackass like Dyce would stay in love with and keep chasing after the same woman for so long.

Lepka

Miyazaki: As I said, I can’t do this work unless I identify with and have some emotional attachment to the characters. I even found myself empathizing with Lepka.

—With Lepka?

Miyazaki: Yes. Dyce was best for us as a bad guy, but as you know he bowed out of that role. That left us with no one else. As the famous Japanese saying goes, “The grains of sand on the beach may one day all disappear, but thieves never will …” Well, it would have been one thing if we had had tons of bad guys in reserve, but if we had eliminated Lepka, we wouldn’t have had anyone left. That’s the way the story was designed. And poor Lepka almost seemed to go mad. He was isolated and on his own. He was struggling on all alone. The nuclear reactor was nearly out; the Gunboat had taken off and not come back. There was no food and the underground residents were up to no good. It would have been enough to drive anyone crazy. And he probably wasn’t the only one going around and branding people with tattoos on their foreheads. He was, to tell the truth, probably at the point where he didn’t know what was going on. I like the idea of a purifying or cathartic effect, and if he had said, “Urotaeruna,” or “Don’t panic, men!” one more time, the show would have become a total manga, a joke. Then I never would have been able to kill him off. Flying on the Giganto, Lepka wanted to conquer the whole world, because all he knew of anything was High Harbor and Plaschip Island. He wanted to control both. [laughs] Of course there wasn’t much to do [laughs], because the only thing he could think was to get the combatants back to harvesting wheat, build a resort, and then go off to search for more survivors. He wasn’t really thinking of conquering the world as we know it, or destroying it. He probably just wanted to find a woman who would love him, but Monsley didn’t seem to meet his standards, or maybe she had already given him the cold shoulder. There were all sorts of ridiculous things being said about him among the production staff; there was a rumor that he was gay. Some people said he had a rather nasty look about him. [laughs]

—Were they thinking of him with Dyce? [laughs]

Miyazaki: Or maybe that he might hook up with Territ. [laughs]

—I thought the Giganto might be used to fight in one more episode …

Miyazaki: But if so, I would have had to clean up Lepka’s character somehow. As I mentioned, if he’d said “Don’t panic!” one more time, he would’ve become a character that I couldn’t have killed off.

—I see what you mean. With one more episode, he would’ve become a character that people couldn’t hate anymore.

Miyazaki: Exactly. And even the way things were, lots of people later made ridiculous comments, saying that Lepka was still alive, that he had arrived on Remnant Island before the others, or even that he was already living in the rocket shed there. With my personality, I couldn’t go on seriously with him, and I wouldn’t have been able to kill him off, either. And it would have made everything I had done in the series up to that point meaningless. It’s probably not a good thing to get too carried away by your own personal inclinations in this sort of project. I’m really not good at depicting the bad guys, frankly. They always wind up to be people who are at the core basically good. I tried so hard not to let Lepka turn out this way. He’s the kind of character who doesn’t even look good in a Western-style suit, because it just makes him look like your ordinary, mean-spirited bureaucrat, that’s all. That’s why I tried so hard to make him look a little “bad” by having him wear combat clothes and showing him with a good physique, with a broad chest. Viewers will actually overlook a lot if a character is usually desperately running around like crazy, consequences be damned.

The cathartic effect of cartoon films

—I’d like to ask you about the cathartic or purifying effect that you mentioned earlier.

Miyazaki: It’s something I like. Take an evil character such as Hilda in Little Norse Prince Valiant. She has a change of heart and at the end she’s done in by the Snow Wolves, isn’t she? If that change of heart hadn’t happened, I can’t imagine anyone ever forgiving her. A purifying effect comes into play when an evil character transforms into a truly happy person, or when some really awful person turns good. It can happen in a variety of situations. For example, in Conan there is the moment when Monsley thinks of dying. When she chucks off everything and decides that she wants to live, not in a world of steel and plastic, but among greenery, she is purified. It was the same with Dyce. When he finally gave up his obsession with the Barracuda, he is able to obtain a real Barracuda for the first time. Of course, when trying to explain something like this in words, I know it starts sounding too formulaic.

In Future Boy Conan, the story ends with everyone becoming very innocent. I think it essentially ends by opening the door to a possible future. The characters are all rejuvenated … It ends with Jimsy being far more childlike than when he first appeared in the story; in the final episode this is true of Lana as well. Even characters like Dyce are totally changed. Monsley becomes more youthful.

In fact, I think they all become much younger. People often say that characters in stories mature, but I don’t think characters in cartoon films mature to become people who, for example, make important-sounding statements. Instead, they are liberated from a variety of constraints. At least, that’s what I want to them to be. Usually they all have something they’re burdened by, like a weird complex, don’t you think? Take the case of Lana; she finally realizes her own honest desire to be with Conan, rather than her grandfather, Lao, and is then able to fly to Conan’s side. And I think, conversely, that this increases her love and respect for Lao.

I feel that viewers should feel liberated after watching cartoon films, and that the characters should also ultimately be liberated. So I like the idea that the Conan characters actually became more innocent at the end.

What really makes me mad about most TV anime, to the extent that I have watched it, is that the shows don’t have any sort of purifying or cathartic effect at all. I really can’t stand them. I think they don’t have any respect for real humanity. The only way they can imagine humans changing is by assuming that people want to change. It’s too terrifying for the creators to deal with characters that seem incapable of changing even as they are changing. At first I considered making Monsley a middle-aged woman—around thirty-five years old, as she is in the original story. I even considered depicting her with sunken cheeks, a nervous disposition, and silver hair. But when we entered the storyboard stage of production, I realized, “Hey, wait a minute, there aren’t any young female characters in this story and a beautiful woman would be good … Let’s make her a beautiful woman!” I think that is why we were ultimately able to save her. If she’d been an old lady, I’m sure she would’ve been much harder to save. Monsley was a woman who wanted to change from the beginning—she was really just going against the grain of her basic nature. So all she needed was an opportunity to change; I think she was able to change because part of her had always wanted to be liberated.

As to the question of why Conan was such a “good kid,” well, I think he was just born a healthy human. I honestly believe there are people like that. After all, Conan conceivably could have become an Orlo type of person. I don’t really know why Orlo changed. People like Orlo sometimes live their whole lives in a twisted fashion. But I didn’t want to leave him like that, so at the end I had him setting off fireworks with old man Gull, suggesting that maybe Gull had spent quite a bit of energy trying to reform this young juvenile delinquent, to the point of even lobbing bombs with him. I thought this would be a somewhat more lighthearted depiction. It’s all too easy to make serious scenes, so I wanted to create something less serious. I think it’s okay to do this, even if it’s not very realistic, even if it’s just wishful thinking.

In cartoon films chase scenes only really become possible when the actions of the characters have all been simplified. When there are still mysteries or problems to be solved, or women to be freed, you can’t have a real chase scene. When all the characters are free, when clear relationships have been established, bad guys have been revealed to be really bad, and we know who must be destroyed, then it’s okay to go wild. In the case of Conan, it took an awfully long time to get to the point where we could do this in a worry-free way, because there was the whole issue of Armageddon in the background.

Leaving aside liking people or not, I do think that all men have a type of admiration for females in general. I personally don’t like wanton women like the Fujiko Mine character in Lupin. But if I happen to see something innocently charming in someone like that, then I think I’ve probably also discovered the real woman in her. It all depends on how I discover this charming aspect. When I’m thinking, “What an awful woman,” and then see something charming about her, I might even fall in love. That’s the purifying effect I’m talking about.

Someday I’d love to create an animated version of Beauty and the Beast. I don’t mean a literal interpretation of the story—I’d really prefer to depict the beast. I’d like to create a film where the character is cleansed by being devoted to something, and is transformed by being cleansed, so that at the end the character becomes what we wish had been there all along.

Among the special qualities animation originally had was the ability to not only make things move, but to transform them spiritually. Yet the instant this quality was incorporated into narrative stories, it nearly disappeared. It’s exactly the sort of thing that I’d love to work on. I’d love to incorporate more of the transformational quality of characters in my animation.

In that sense, I feel as though I understand Charlie Chaplin well. People go on and on about the machine-centered civilization depicted in Modern Times, but I don’t think Chaplin himself made the film because he was particularly interested in that subject. I think the film really depicts an earnest sort of admiration for women, and a special sort of gentleness. When the woman Chaplin admires appears in the film, he feels that he can ennoble himself by being devoted to her, and this aspiration of his, you might say, permeates the entire film. It’s the reason I really love the film’s ending.

In search of a cartoon movie

—What does making a “cartoon movie” mean to you?

Miyazaki: I just want to make films I want to see. I think that cartoon movies above all help our spirits relax, they make us feel happy, and they make us feel refreshed. And while doing so, they may also allow us to escape from ourselves … We live trapped in ourselves, imprisoned in the real world. But if we can free ourselves from the various complexes we have and the tangled relationships we are in to live in a freer, more open world, we might be able to become strong and heroic. I think everyone entertains thoughts of becoming more beautiful, or more gentle, or of having a more meaningful existence. Everyone, whether young or old, man or woman.

I like the expression “lost possibilities.” To be born means being compelled to choose an era, a place, and a life. To exist here, now, means to lose the possibility of being countless other potential selves. For example, I might have been the captain of a pirate ship, sailing with a lovely princess by my side. It means giving up this universe, giving up other potential selves. There are selves which are lost possibilities, and selves that could have been, and this is not limited just to us but to the people around us and even to Japan itself.

Yet once born there is no turning back. And I think that’s exactly why the fantasy worlds of cartoon movies so strongly represent our hopes and yearnings. They illustrate a world of lost possibilities for us. And in this sense I think that the animation we see today often lacks the vitality of older cartoon movies. Economic constraints in production are often said to be the main reason, but it seems to me that something spiritual is also missing. It would be stupid to turn my back on the times in which we live and act arrogant about it all, but I always find myself thinking that the old cartoon movies were indeed more interesting and exciting than what we have today.

—I like cartoon movies, too, but I sometimes think they’re a way of escaping from reality.

Miyazaki: It’s true that they’re a form of escapism. Cartoons are a fake world. Because cartoons are fake, they disarm viewers, making them think that they’re “just cartoons.” Liberated from reality and relaxed, viewers find themselves pulled into scenes showing the protagonists and a cartoon world and then may find that the experience evokes secret hopes and longings in themselves. They may start feeling braver and more heroic, more generous in spirit. And then they may also find that they feel a little more energized, or that their lover’s face looks even prettier than it did before.

—I know many in the industry hate it when they hear people disparagingly say things like, “Hmph. Just a bunch of cartoons …”

Miyazaki: I know. But I think this is what they’re supposed to be. Cartoon films aren’t meant to expound on complex themes or theories, and I don’t think there’s any need to insist on them being art, either. They start out being preposterous, so it’s all right to depict absurd settings or tell bald lies—viewers accept this. But the creators still need to try hard to make their fake worlds seem as real as possible. It’s not good enough to just string together a bunch of clever ideas, for the effort required is fundamentally different. Lies must be layered upon lies to create a thoroughly believable fake world. It’s an imaginary world, but it should seem to actually exist as an alternate world, and the people who live there should appear to think and act in a realistic way. This can be a truly ridiculous line of work, but when depicting a world with three suns, you have to construct a world that will seem to the viewers like it could have three suns. I think the trick here is turning the lies you create into a single, coherent world.

—So it’s a trick, not an art?

Miyazaki: Yes, it’s a trick. The viewers know that what they are seeing is fake, that it can’t be reality, but at the same time they sense deep in their hearts that there is some sort of truth in the work. This, at least, is the sort of cartoon film I really want to make.

—And speaking of the animated works you would like to make, can you be more specific?

Miyazaki: Well, in today’s world if you try to create an adventure film, you run into an awful lot of problems, at least from the storytelling aspect. Films based on children’s literature have sometimes done quite well, but we’re always discussing among ourselves whether we can really create a story where children discover things by themselves anymore. It’s not an easy thing to do, especially in today’s Japan where we have so many concrete walls and streets filled with cars and trucks. And sometimes it’s hard to get an idea for an original project approved. Of course, I think that since we’re creating a fake world anyway, that we ought to be able to forget about all these constraints and present a world where we’re free to run riot. So then people say, “Well, do a love story.” Now, I’ve worked all these years with Paku-san and haven’t been able to become fully involved in love stories, so that actually makes me want to make them even more.

I hate the fact that in From the Apennines to the Andes, for example, we had Marco and Fiolina run to each other but not embrace. Marco’s mother and Fiolina hug one another, so why shouldn’t Marco and Fiolina? While laying out the story, I kept thinking that they should hold each other tightly, because it seemed even more suggestive to have them holding hands and staring into each other’s eyes. I didn’t want to stop them from moving, however, so I found myself with no choice but to make them hold hands and twirl about. Whether in cartoon movies or in a physical representation, it seems to me that when showing people truly happy it’s best to show them hugging. So then why not make a real love story? I don’t know why Lana washes up on Remnant Island. Only one out of tens of thousands of people comes across his or her true love by sheer accident. And if so, I thought it would be possible for Conan to have it happen to him. I thought it would be wonderful to have such a fateful meeting. Remember how Jimsy expressed his envy of Conan? Well, we’re all like Jimsy.

—Some people think that having groups of people collaborate to make cartoon films is stupid.

Miyazaki: Let them say that. Works by those creating “experimental animation” or by individuals creating animation on their own are like a type of haiku that makes you marvel at how much time the poet spent in its creation all based on a single flash of inspiration. But there’s also room for a different world, where large groups of people work together to create films. There’s an unforgettable thrill involved in this.

To me, the most interesting thing about real cartoon films is that you create a world, you fully exploit the space in it, and then you create the kishōtenketsu, or logical structure of a beginning, a development, a twist, and a conclusion. This is the most fun to watch, and what I find motivates me the most. Cartoon films are fake. And because they’re fake, you can tell a big fib, but I always like it when it seems like there’s also a bit of truth in the fibs. I’ve recently come to the conclusion that I’m not very good at lying though, and that I’ll have to work on it so I can tell a great big lie someday. I’ve been making animated films for a long time, but when I compare what I’ve done with films that have really impressed me in the past, I have to ask myself if I’ve been able to surpass them. Then the answer is no. I’ve just adapted the technology and methods used by older films to our times. A lot of people around me have given up, believing that we’ll never be able to do anything better, but I still believe that, given the right opportunities, we might be able to. You might only see one cartoon film a year, but the imagery in it would be so beautiful it might seem to surpass the real world. Children watching it might forget the story completely and remember only one certain scene, as if it were a beautiful, shiny treasure. Even if they were to see it again as adults and find it didn’t really amount to much, they would still want it to be the way they remembered it. This is probably because it is something that has been personally experienced. But I think any works that have so much energy put into their creation should qualify for this sort of treatment. They shouldn’t be something created just to sell merchandise, or be cranked-out fluff like toilet paper; they should be worthy of emotional investment, and when they have been visualized and displayed on the screen, they should seem like a work into which someone has put a lot of energy. It should be apparent that the creators tried to add something new and different.

—In conclusion, does Conan work for you as a cartoon film?

Miyazaki: No. I mean I’ve made a variety of films, but I don’t think I’ve done any work yet where I’ve truly managed to create a whole world. That is, compared to the cartoon films that have impressed me so much in the past. Compared to our predecessors who pioneered cartoon films, I sometimes feel as though we’re just using the technologies and techniques that they came up with to create their own worlds, adapting these to our times, and doing it in a cheap way. The economic conditions are tough, because the theater hardly functions as a market these days, but I’m not ready to give up … I want to create the sort of film that a young boy sees in a theater and then goes home from so amazed he’s temporarily rendered speechless; he doesn’t say anything to anyone out of fear that he’ll dilute the experience. I want to make a film that creates such a sense of yearning and admiration that it brings people to tears. That’s the sort of film I’d like to make someday.

—And we’d love to have you make it.
